Numbers 1.summary: In the wilderness of Sinai, the LORD tells Moses to count every man twenty years old and up who can go to war (Numbers 1:1–4). A leader from each tribe is named to help (Numbers 1:5–16). Tribe by tribe the men are counted, for a total of 603,550 (Numbers 1:17–46). The Levites are not counted with them, because they are set apart to carry and guard the tabernacle (Numbers 1:47–54).
Numbers 1.whereWeAre: Leviticus ended with Israel still camped at Mount Sinai. Numbers begins one month after the tabernacle was set up, as God tells Moses to count the men who can fight. Chapter 2 arranges the tribes around the tabernacle.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Tells Moses to count the men who can go to war.

keyFigures.name: Moses and Aaron
keyFigures.role: Count the people with the help of the tribal leaders.

keyFigures.name: The tribal leaders
keyFigures.role: One man from each tribe, named to help with the count.

keyFigures.name: The Levites
keyFigures.role: Set apart to carry and guard the tabernacle instead.

keyThemes.explanation: Each tribe is counted by name and family as Israel gets ready to travel.
The Levites serve at the tabernacle while the other tribes prepare to fight.
The Levites camp around the tabernacle so that no one comes near it carelessly.

Numbers 2.summary: Each tribe is to camp under its own standard around the tabernacle (Numbers 2:1–2). Judah, Issachar, and Zebulun camp on the east and lead the march (Numbers 2:3–9), with Reuben's camp on the south (Numbers 2:10–16). The Levites and the tabernacle travel in the middle (Numbers 2:17). Ephraim's camp is on the west (Numbers 2:18–24) and Dan's on the north (Numbers 2:25–31). Israel camps and marches just as the LORD commanded (Numbers 2:32–34).
Numbers 2.whereWeAre: Chapter 1 counted Israel's fighting men, tribe by tribe. Now God arranges where each tribe camps and marches, with the tabernacle in the middle. Chapters 3–4 turn to the tribe of Levi, which camps closest to it.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Gives each tribe its place around the tabernacle.

keyFigures.name: Moses and Aaron
keyFigures.role: Receive the plan for the camp.

keyFigures.name: The twelve tribes
keyFigures.role: Camp and march under their own standards.

keyFigures.name: The Levites
keyFigures.role: Camp around the tabernacle and travel in the middle.

keyThemes.explanation: The tabernacle stands in the middle, with every tribe camped around it.
Each tribe knows where to camp and when to march.
"And the children of Israel did according to all that the LORD commanded Moses."

Numbers 3.summary: Aaron's sons are named as priests, and the chapter recalls how Nadab and Abihu died for offering "strange fire" (Numbers 3:1–4). The LORD gives the Levites to serve Aaron and takes them in place of Israel's firstborn (Numbers 3:5–13). The Levites are counted, and each clan is given its place around the tabernacle and its work (Numbers 3:14–39). There are 273 more firstborn than Levites, so each extra one is bought back for five shekels (Numbers 3:40–51).
Numbers 3.whereWeAre: Chapters 1–2 counted and arranged the twelve tribes but left out Levi. This chapter counts the Levites and gives them to serve the priests, in place of Israel's firstborn sons. Chapter 4 gives each Levite family its job in moving the tabernacle.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Takes the Levites as his own in place of Israel's firstborn.

keyFigures.name: Moses
keyFigures.role: Counts the Levites and collects the money to buy back the extra firstborn.

keyFigures.name: Aaron and his sons
keyFigures.role: The priests, whom the Levites will serve.

keyFigures.name: The Gershonites, Kohathites, and Merarites
keyFigures.role: The three Levite clans, each given a place and a duty.

keyThemes.explanation: Only those God chooses may serve as priests.
The Levites belong to the LORD in place of Israel's firstborn.
Every extra firstborn is bought back with silver.

Numbers 4.summary: The Kohathites, aged thirty to fifty, carry the holy things, but only after the priests have covered them, for they must not touch or see them (Numbers 4:1–20). The Gershonites carry the curtains and coverings (Numbers 4:21–28), and the Merarites carry the boards, bars, and pillars (Numbers 4:29–33). The Levites who can serve are counted: 8,580 in all (Numbers 4:34–49).
Numbers 4.whereWeAre: Chapter 3 counted all the Levites. This chapter counts the men aged thirty to fifty and gives each family its part in carrying the tabernacle. With the camp in order, chapters 5–6 turn to keeping it pure.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Gives each Levite family its work.

keyFigures.name: Moses and Aaron
keyFigures.role: Count the Levites who can serve.

keyFigures.name: The Kohathites
keyFigures.role: Carry the holy things once the priests have covered them.

keyFigures.name: The Gershonites
keyFigures.role: Carry the curtains and coverings.

keyFigures.name: The Merarites
keyFigures.role: Carry the boards, bars, and pillars.

keyFigures.name: Eleazar and Ithamar
keyFigures.role: Aaron's sons, who oversee the work.

keyThemes.explanation: The priests cover the holy things so the Kohathites can carry them safely.
Each Levite family carries its own part of the tabernacle.
The Levites are counted by the work they do.

Numbers 5.summary: Anyone with leprosy, a discharge, or contact with the dead must stay outside the camp (Numbers 5:1–4). A person who wrongs another must confess and pay it back with a fifth added (Numbers 5:5–10). If a husband suspects his wife of adultery with no witness, the priest has her drink bitter water before the LORD, and God shows whether she is guilty (Numbers 5:11–31).
Numbers 5.whereWeAre: The camp has been counted and arranged in chapters 1–4. Now God gives laws to keep it clean and honest, since he lives in the middle of it. Chapter 6 continues with the Nazirite vow and the priestly blessing.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Gives laws to keep the camp clean and set wrongs right.

keyFigures.name: Moses
keyFigures.role: Passes the laws on to Israel.

keyFigures.name: The priest
keyFigures.role: Gives the bitter water to a wife accused without a witness.

keyThemes.explanation: The camp must stay clean because God lives in the middle of it.
Confession must come with paying back what was taken.
When no one saw what happened, the case is brought before God.

Numbers 6.summary: Any man or woman may take the vow of a Nazarite, giving up wine and grapes, letting the hair grow, and staying away from the dead (Numbers 6:1–8). If someone dies beside him, he starts his vow over (Numbers 6:9–12). When the vow ends, he brings offerings and shaves his head (Numbers 6:13–21). The chapter ends with the priestly blessing: "The LORD bless thee, and keep thee" (Numbers 6:22–27).
Numbers 6.whereWeAre: Chapter 5 gave laws for keeping the camp pure. This chapter describes the Nazirite vow, a way for any man or woman to be set apart for God for a time. It ends with the priestly blessing, before chapter 7 steps back to the day the tabernacle was finished.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Gives the vow of the Nazarite and the words of the priestly blessing.

keyFigures.name: Moses
keyFigures.role: Passes the laws on to Israel.

keyFigures.name: Aaron and his sons
keyFigures.role: Told to bless Israel in the LORD's name.

keyThemes.explanation: Any man or woman may choose to be set apart to God for a time.
If a Nazarite is made unclean by accident, he begins his vow again.
"The LORD make his face shine upon thee, and be gracious unto thee."

Numbers 7.summary: On the day the tabernacle is set up, the tribal leaders bring six wagons and twelve oxen to carry it (Numbers 7:1–9). For twelve days, one leader each day brings the same gift for the altar (Numbers 7:10–83). The gifts are added up (Numbers 7:84–88). When Moses goes into the tabernacle, he hears God's voice "from off the mercy seat" (Numbers 7:89).
Numbers 7.whereWeAre: This chapter steps back to the day the tabernacle was set up at the end of Exodus, a month before the census in chapter 1. Over twelve days, each tribe's leader brings the same gifts for the altar. Chapter 8 turns to the lamps and to setting apart the Levites.

keyFigures.name: The tribal leaders
keyFigures.role: Bring wagons, oxen, and twelve days of gifts for the altar.

keyFigures.name: Moses
keyFigures.role: Gives the wagons to the Levites and hears God's voice in the tabernacle.

keyFigures.name: The Gershonites and Merarites
keyFigures.role: Receive the wagons for carrying their loads.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Speaks to Moses from above the mercy seat.

keyThemes.explanation: Each tribe brings the same gift, so every tribe shares equally in worship.
The wagons go to the Levites with the heaviest loads.
Moses hears God's voice from above the mercy seat.

Numbers 8.summary: Aaron lights the seven lamps so that they shine forward (Numbers 8:1–4). The Levites are cleansed, the people lay their hands on them, and they are given to the LORD in place of the firstborn (Numbers 8:5–22). They serve from age twenty-five to fifty, then help the younger men (Numbers 8:23–26).
Numbers 8.whereWeAre: Chapter 7 recorded the tribes' gifts for the altar. Now Aaron sets up the lamps, and the Levites are cleansed and given to God for their work. Chapter 9 tells of the Passover kept just before Israel leaves Sinai.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Tells Moses how to set the Levites apart.

keyFigures.name: Aaron
keyFigures.role: Lights the lamps and offers the Levites before the LORD.

keyFigures.name: The Levites
keyFigures.role: Are cleansed and given to the LORD for their work.

keyFigures.name: The children of Israel
keyFigures.role: Lay their hands on the Levites.

keyThemes.explanation: The Levites are cleansed before they begin their work.
The Levites serve on behalf of the whole people.
Older Levites step back from heavy work and help the younger ones.

Numbers 9.summary: In the first month of the second year, Israel keeps the Passover at Sinai (Numbers 9:1–5). Some men are unclean from touching a dead body, so God lets anyone unclean or far away keep it a month later (Numbers 9:6–14). From then on the cloud over the tabernacle tells Israel when to camp and when to travel (Numbers 9:15–23).
Numbers 9.whereWeAre: The Levites were set apart in chapter 8. This chapter tells of the first Passover since leaving Egypt, kept at Sinai one year later, and explains how the cloud will guide Israel. In chapter 10 the cloud lifts, and the journey begins.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Lets those who were unclean keep the Passover a month later.

keyFigures.name: Moses
keyFigures.role: Asks the LORD what the unclean men should do.

keyFigures.name: The unclean men
keyFigures.role: Ask why they must miss the Passover.

keyFigures.name: The children of Israel
keyFigures.role: Camp and travel at the LORD's command.

keyThemes.explanation: Those who missed the Passover may keep it a month later.
The stranger keeps the Passover by the same law as the Israelite.
"At the commandment of the LORD they rested in the tents."

Numbers 10.summary: God has Moses make two silver trumpets to call the people and to signal the march (Numbers 10:1–10). On the twentieth day of the second month the cloud lifts, and the tribes leave Sinai in order (Numbers 10:11–28). Moses asks his relative Hobab to come and guide them (Numbers 10:29–32). As the ark sets out, Moses prays, "Rise up, LORD, and let thine enemies be scattered" (Numbers 10:33–36).
Numbers 10.whereWeAre: Israel has been camped at Mount Sinai for almost a year, since Exodus 19. Now the trumpets sound, the cloud lifts, and the tribes set out in order toward the promised land. The journey goes wrong almost at once in chapter 11.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Tells Moses to make the trumpets and lifts the cloud from the tabernacle.

keyFigures.name: Moses
keyFigures.role: Leads the march and prays as the ark sets out and stops.

keyFigures.name: Aaron's sons, the priests
keyFigures.role: Blow the silver trumpets.

keyFigures.name: Hobab
keyFigures.role: Moses' relative, asked to guide Israel in the wilderness.

keyFigures.name: The tribes
keyFigures.role: March out of Sinai in their order.

keyThemes.explanation: The silver trumpets call the people together and signal the march.
Israel leaves Sinai only when the cloud lifts.
Moses prays each time the ark sets out and each time it stops.

Numbers 11.summary: The people complain, and fire burns at the edge of the camp until Moses prays; the place is called Taberah (Numbers 11:1–3). They cry for meat, and Moses tells God the burden is too heavy for him (Numbers 11:4–15). God puts his Spirit on seventy elders, and even Eldad and Medad prophesy in the camp (Numbers 11:16–30). Quail cover the ground, but a plague strikes the greedy, and the place is named Kibrothhattaavah (Numbers 11:31–35).
Numbers 11.whereWeAre: Israel has just left Sinai in chapter 10, ready to march to the promised land. Only three days out, the people start complaining. Moses is worn out, and in chapter 12 even his own brother and sister turn against him.

keyFigures.name: The people
keyFigures.role: Complain about the hardships and cry for meat.

keyFigures.name: Moses
keyFigures.role: Tells God the load is too heavy and prays for the people.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Sends fire, gives his Spirit to the elders, and sends quail and a plague.

keyFigures.name: The seventy elders
keyFigures.role: Receive the Spirit to help carry the load.

keyFigures.name: Eldad and Medad
keyFigures.role: Prophesy in the camp.

keyFigures.name: Joshua
keyFigures.role: Wants Moses to stop them.

keyThemes.explanation: The people remember Egypt's food and forget Egypt's slavery.
God gives his Spirit to seventy elders so that Moses does not carry the people alone.
God sends quail, but greed brings a plague.

Numbers 12.summary: Miriam and Aaron speak against Moses because of his wife, a Cushite, and ask whether God speaks only through him (Numbers 12:1–3). The LORD calls them to the tabernacle and says he speaks with Moses "mouth to mouth" (Numbers 12:4–9). Miriam becomes leprous, Moses prays for her healing, and she waits outside the camp seven days (Numbers 12:10–16).
Numbers 12.whereWeAre: The people complained about food in chapter 11. Now Miriam and Aaron, Moses' own sister and brother, question his leadership. God defends Moses, and in chapter 13 Israel stands at the edge of Canaan.

keyFigures.name: Miriam
keyFigures.role: Speaks against Moses and becomes leprous.

keyFigures.name: Aaron
keyFigures.role: Joins her, then begs Moses to help her.

keyFigures.name: Moses
keyFigures.role: Prays, "Heal her now, O God, I beseech thee."

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Defends Moses and rebukes Miriam and Aaron.

keyThemes.explanation: Moses is "very meek," and God himself defends him.
Miriam and Aaron's jealousy brings God's rebuke.
Moses prays for the sister who spoke against him.

Numbers 13.summary: Moses sends twelve men, one from each tribe, to spy out Canaan, and he renames Oshea as Joshua (Numbers 13:1–20). They search the land for forty days and carry back a huge cluster of grapes from Eshcol (Numbers 13:21–25). They report a land of milk and honey but strong, walled cities; Caleb says, "we are well able to overcome it," but the others say they were like grasshoppers (Numbers 13:26–33).
Numbers 13.whereWeAre: Israel has traveled from Sinai to the wilderness of Paran, on the edge of the promised land. Moses sends twelve men to spy out Canaan. Ten of them come back afraid, and chapter 14 tells how the people respond.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Tells Moses to send men to search Canaan.

keyFigures.name: Moses
keyFigures.role: Sends the twelve spies and renames Oshea as Joshua.

keyFigures.name: Caleb
keyFigures.role: Urges Israel to go up at once and take the land.

keyFigures.name: Joshua
keyFigures.role: One of the twelve spies.

keyFigures.name: The ten spies
keyFigures.role: Say Israel cannot win and spread a frightening report.

keyThemes.explanation: The land is rich, but its cities are strong and its people are big.
Caleb says, "Let us go up at once, and possess it."
Ten spies see themselves as grasshoppers, and their fear spreads to the people.

Numbers 14.summary: The people weep, want to choose a captain to lead them back to Egypt, and try to stone Joshua and Caleb (Numbers 14:1–10). God threatens to destroy them, but Moses pleads, "Pardon, I beseech thee, the iniquity of this people" (Numbers 14:11–25). God forgives, but that generation will wander forty years and die in the wilderness, except Caleb and Joshua (Numbers 14:26–38). The next day the people attack anyway and are beaten back to Hormah (Numbers 14:39–45).
Numbers 14.whereWeAre: Chapter 13 ended with ten spies saying Israel cannot win. Now the people refuse to go in, and God says that generation will wander in the wilderness for forty years and die there. This is the turning point of Numbers; chapters 15–19 belong to the long years that follow.

keyFigures.name: The people
keyFigures.role: Weep, plan to go back to Egypt, and try to stone Joshua and Caleb.

keyFigures.name: Moses and Aaron
keyFigures.role: Fall on their faces before the people.

keyFigures.name: Joshua and Caleb
keyFigures.role: Plead with the people to trust the LORD.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Forgives the people but sentences them to forty years in the wilderness.

keyFigures.name: The ten spies
keyFigures.role: Die in a plague for their evil report.

keyFigures.name: The Amalekites and Canaanites
keyFigures.role: Beat back Israel's attack.

keyThemes.explanation: The people would rather go back to Egypt than trust God.
God pardons the people, but that generation will not enter the land.
When the people attack without God, they are beaten.

explainedReferences.explanation: Moses repeats God's description of himself as longsuffering, merciful, and forgiving in his intercession.

Numbers 15.summary: God gives laws for offerings "When ye be come into the land," with one law for Israelites and strangers (Numbers 15:1–16). A cake from the first dough is to be given to the LORD (Numbers 15:17–21). Sins done in ignorance can be forgiven, but a person who sins "presumptuously" is cut off (Numbers 15:22–31). A man gathering sticks on the Sabbath is stoned (Numbers 15:32–36), and Israel is told to wear fringes with a blue thread to remember God's commands (Numbers 15:37–41).
Numbers 15.whereWeAre: Israel has just refused to enter the land and been sentenced to forty years in the wilderness. Yet God gives laws that begin, "When ye be come into the land" (Numbers 15:2), a promise that their children will get there. Chapter 16 tells of a rebellion against Moses and Aaron.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Gives laws for life in the land and judges the Sabbath-breaker.

keyFigures.name: Moses
keyFigures.role: Brings the case of the Sabbath-breaker to the LORD.

keyFigures.name: The man gathering sticks
keyFigures.role: Breaks the Sabbath and is stoned.

keyFigures.name: The congregation
keyFigures.role: Carries out the sentence.

keyThemes.explanation: God gives laws for the land even after Israel's refusal.
Sins done in ignorance can be forgiven, but open defiance cuts a person off.
The fringes on their clothes remind Israel to "remember, and do all my commandments."

Numbers 16.summary: Korah, a Levite, joins Dathan, Abiram, and 250 leaders to challenge Moses and Aaron (Numbers 16:1–11). Dathan and Abiram refuse Moses' call to come (Numbers 16:12–15). The earth opens and swallows the rebels, and fire burns up the 250 men offering incense (Numbers 16:16–35). Their censers are beaten into a covering for the altar as a warning (Numbers 16:36–40). When the people grumble, a plague begins, and Aaron stands "between the dead and the living" with incense until it stops (Numbers 16:41–50).
Numbers 16.whereWeAre: The wandering years have begun after Israel's refusal in chapter 14. Now Korah and other leaders rise up against Moses and Aaron and claim the right to be priests. God judges them, and chapter 17 settles the question of whom God has chosen.

keyFigures.name: Korah
keyFigures.role: A Levite who leads the rebellion against Moses and Aaron.

keyFigures.name: Dathan and Abiram
keyFigures.role: Reubenites who refuse to come when Moses calls them.

keyFigures.name: The 250 leaders
keyFigures.role: Offer incense and are burned up.

keyFigures.name: Moses
keyFigures.role: Leaves the choice to the LORD and pleads for the people.

keyFigures.name: Aaron
keyFigures.role: Stands between the dead and the living with incense.

keyFigures.name: Eleazar
keyFigures.role: Gathers the censers to make a covering for the altar.

keyThemes.explanation: Korah and his followers want a role God has not given them.
Offering incense without God's call brings judgment.
Aaron runs into the crowd with incense, and the plague stops.

Numbers 17.summary: God has each tribe's leader bring a rod with his name on it and lays them in the tabernacle (Numbers 17:1–7). By morning Aaron's rod has budded, blossomed, and borne almonds, and it is kept as a sign against rebels (Numbers 17:8–11). The people cry out that they are all about to die (Numbers 17:12–13).
Numbers 17.whereWeAre: Korah's rebellion in chapter 16 asked who has the right to serve as priest. God answers with a sign: of twelve staffs, only Aaron's buds overnight. The people are now afraid to come near the tabernacle, and chapter 18 answers that fear.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Chooses Aaron by making his rod bud.

keyFigures.name: Moses
keyFigures.role: Gathers the rods and lays them before the LORD.

keyFigures.name: Aaron
keyFigures.role: His rod buds, blossoms, and bears almonds.

keyFigures.name: The tribal leaders
keyFigures.role: Each bring a rod with his name on it.

keyFigures.name: The people
keyFigures.role: Cry out that they will all die.

keyThemes.explanation: Aaron's rod buds to show whom God has chosen.
The rod is kept as a warning against rebellion.
The people are afraid to come near the tabernacle.

Numbers 18.summary: The priests and Levites are made responsible for guarding the tabernacle, so that no one else comes near and dies (Numbers 18:1–7). The priests receive portions of the offerings and firstfruits, and the LORD tells Aaron, "I am thy part and thine inheritance" (Numbers 18:8–20). The Levites receive Israel's tithes in place of land (Numbers 18:21–24), and they give a tenth of those tithes to the priests (Numbers 18:25–32).
Numbers 18.whereWeAre: Chapter 17 ended with the people afraid that anyone who comes near the tabernacle will die. God answers by making the priests and Levites responsible for guarding it. He also explains how they will be supported, before chapter 19 turns to cleansing after contact with death.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Tells Aaron how the priests and Levites will guard the tabernacle and be supported.

keyFigures.name: Aaron and his sons
keyFigures.role: Serve as priests and receive their share of the offerings.

keyFigures.name: The Levites
keyFigures.role: Help the priests and receive Israel's tithes.

keyThemes.explanation: The priests must answer for any wrong done at the sanctuary.
The people's offerings and tithes support those who serve.
Even the Levites give a tenth of what they receive.

Numbers 19.summary: A red heifer without blemish is burned outside the camp, and its ashes are kept for the water of cleansing (Numbers 19:1–10). Anyone who touches a dead body is unclean for seven days and must be sprinkled with this water on the third and seventh days (Numbers 19:11–22).
Numbers 19.whereWeAre: Chapters 16–18 were full of death, from Korah's rebellion to the plague that followed. This chapter explains how a person is made clean after touching a dead body, using the ashes of a red heifer. Chapter 20 jumps ahead to the end of the forty years.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Gives the law of the red heifer.

keyFigures.name: Moses and Aaron
keyFigures.role: Receive the law.

keyFigures.name: Eleazar
keyFigures.role: Takes the heifer outside the camp and sprinkles its blood.

keyFigures.name: A clean man
keyFigures.role: Gathers the ashes and sprinkles the water.

keyThemes.explanation: Touching a dead body makes a person unclean for seven days.
The water with the heifer's ashes makes a person clean again.
Anyone who refuses to be cleansed defiles the sanctuary.

Numbers 20.summary: At Kadesh, Miriam dies; when the people complain of thirst, God tells Moses to speak to the rock, but Moses strikes it twice in anger, and God says he will not bring Israel into the land (Numbers 20:1–13). The king of Edom refuses to let Israel pass through his land (Numbers 20:14–21). On mount Hor, Aaron's garments are put on Eleazar, and Aaron dies (Numbers 20:22–29).
Numbers 20.whereWeAre: The forty years in the wilderness are nearly over, and the people are back at Kadesh. Miriam dies, Moses strikes the rock in anger and loses his place in the promised land, and Aaron dies on Mount Hor. In chapter 21 Israel finally begins to move toward Canaan from the east.

keyFigures.name: Miriam
keyFigures.role: Dies at Kadesh.

keyFigures.name: The people
keyFigures.role: Complain that there is no water.

keyFigures.name: Moses
keyFigures.role: Strikes the rock twice instead of speaking to it.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Gives water but tells Moses and Aaron they will not enter the land.

keyFigures.name: The king of Edom
keyFigures.role: Refuses to let Israel pass.

keyFigures.name: Aaron and Eleazar
keyFigures.role: Aaron dies on mount Hor, and his son takes his place.

keyThemes.explanation: Even Moses and Aaron are judged for disobeying God.
God still gives water to a complaining people.
Aaron's garments pass to Eleazar as one generation gives way to the next.

Numbers 21.summary: Israel defeats the Canaanite king of Arad (Numbers 21:1–3). When the people complain again, fiery serpents bite them, and Moses makes "a serpent of brass" so that anyone who looks at it lives (Numbers 21:4–9). They travel north and sing to a well God gives them (Numbers 21:10–20). Israel defeats Sihon king of the Amorites (Numbers 21:21–32) and Og king of Bashan (Numbers 21:33–35).
Numbers 21.whereWeAre: Chapter 20 ended with Aaron's death and Edom refusing to let Israel pass. Israel goes around Edom, complains again, and is saved by looking at a bronze serpent, which Jesus later compares to his own death (John 3:14). Then they win their first victories east of the Jordan and camp on the plains of Moab, where chapters 22–36 take place.

keyFigures.name: The king of Arad
keyFigures.role: Attacks Israel and is defeated.

keyFigures.name: The people
keyFigures.role: Complain, are bitten by serpents, and confess their sin.

keyFigures.name: Moses
keyFigures.role: Prays and makes the serpent of brass.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Sends the serpents and gives the cure.

keyFigures.name: Sihon
keyFigures.role: King of the Amorites, defeated when he attacks.

keyFigures.name: Og
keyFigures.role: King of Bashan, defeated when he attacks.

keyThemes.explanation: The people call the manna "this light bread," and serpents come among them.
Anyone bitten who looks at the serpent of brass lives (John 3:14).
Israel defeats Sihon and Og and takes land east of the Jordan.

explainedReferences.explanation: Jesus explicitly recalls Moses lifting up the serpent in the wilderness.

Numbers 22.summary: Israel camps in the plains of Moab, and Balak king of Moab sends for Balaam to curse them, but God tells Balaam not to go (Numbers 22:1–14). Balak sends greater princes, and God lets Balaam go but only to speak his word (Numbers 22:15–21). On the road, Balaam's ass sees the angel of the LORD, turns aside three times, and speaks to him (Numbers 22:22–35). Balaam meets Balak, who offers sacrifices (Numbers 22:36–41).
Numbers 22.whereWeAre: Israel has just defeated Sihon and Og and is camped on the plains of Moab. Balak, king of Moab, is terrified and hires the prophet Balaam to curse them. In chapters 23–24, Balaam tries.

keyFigures.name: Balak
keyFigures.role: King of Moab, who sends for Balaam to curse Israel.

keyFigures.name: Balaam
keyFigures.role: A seer who may only speak what God tells him.

keyFigures.name: Balaam's ass
keyFigures.role: Sees the angel, turns aside, and speaks.

keyFigures.name: The angel of the LORD
keyFigures.role: Stands in the road with a drawn sword.

keyFigures.name: The princes of Moab
keyFigures.role: Carry Balak's message and money.

keyThemes.explanation: Balak is terrified because of how many Israelites there are.
Balaam can say only what God puts in his mouth.
The ass sees the angel that the famous seer cannot.

Numbers 23.summary: Balaam has seven altars built, but his first message blesses Israel: "How shall I curse, whom God hath not cursed?" (Numbers 23:1–12). Balak tries again from Pisgah, and Balaam says, "God is not a man, that he should lie" (Numbers 23:13–26). Balak takes him to the top of Peor for a third try (Numbers 23:27–30).
Numbers 23.whereWeAre: Balaam arrived in Moab at the end of chapter 22, warned to say only what God tells him. Balak takes him to high places overlooking Israel, but each time Balaam opens his mouth, he blesses instead of curses. Balak tries again in chapter 24.

keyFigures.name: Balak
keyFigures.role: Builds altars and takes Balaam to high places to curse Israel.

keyFigures.name: Balaam
keyFigures.role: Speaks the words God gives him and blesses Israel.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Puts his word in Balaam's mouth.

keyThemes.explanation: Altars and money cannot make Balaam curse Israel.
"God is not a man, that he should lie."
Balaam must speak only what the LORD gives him.

Numbers 24.summary: The Spirit of God comes on Balaam, and he blesses Israel again: "How goodly are thy tents, O Jacob" (Numbers 24:1–9). Balak is furious that Balaam has blessed them three times (Numbers 24:10–14). Balaam sees far ahead: "there shall come a Star out of Jacob" (Numbers 24:15–19). He speaks of other nations and goes home (Numbers 24:20–25).
Numbers 24.whereWeAre: Balaam has blessed Israel twice in chapter 23. Now he blesses them a third time and sees far into the future: "there shall come a Star out of Jacob, and a Sceptre shall rise out of Israel" (Numbers 24:17). Balak sends him home, but chapter 25 shows Israel bringing trouble on itself.

keyFigures.name: Balaam
keyFigures.role: Blesses Israel a third time and sees a Star coming out of Jacob.

keyFigures.name: Balak
keyFigures.role: Is furious and sends Balaam away.

keyFigures.name: The Spirit of God
keyFigures.role: Comes on Balaam as he looks at Israel's camp.

keyThemes.explanation: Every attempt to curse Israel ends in a blessing.
"There shall come a Star out of Jacob, and a Sceptre shall rise out of Israel."
Balak's anger cannot change God's message.

Numbers 25.summary: At Shittim, Israel's men sin with the women of Moab and worship Baalpeor, and a plague breaks out; Phinehas kills Zimri and the Midianite woman Cozbi, and the plague stops after 24,000 have died (Numbers 25:1–9). God gives Phinehas "my covenant of peace," a lasting priesthood (Numbers 25:10–15). God tells Moses to treat the Midianites as enemies (Numbers 25:16–18).
Numbers 25.whereWeAre: Balaam could not curse Israel in chapters 22–24, but Israel falls into sin on its own. The men join in Moab's sexual sin and worship of Baal of Peor, and a plague breaks out. Numbers 31:16 later says this was Balaam's idea, and chapter 26 counts the people who are left.

keyFigures.name: The men of Israel
keyFigures.role: Sin with the women of Moab and worship Baalpeor.

keyFigures.name: Moses
keyFigures.role: Orders the judges to punish those who joined Baalpeor.

keyFigures.name: Phinehas
keyFigures.role: Aaron's grandson, who stops the plague and is promised a lasting priesthood.

keyFigures.name: Zimri and Cozbi
keyFigures.role: An Israelite leader and a Midianite woman, killed by Phinehas.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Sends the plague and makes his covenant of peace with Phinehas.

keyThemes.explanation: Israel's men join in Moab's sin and worship Baalpeor.
Phinehas acts for God's honor, and God makes his covenant of peace with him.
Twenty-four thousand die in the plague.

Numbers 26.summary: After the plague, God tells Moses and Eleazar to count the men again (Numbers 26:1–4). The tribes are counted by families, for a total of 601,730 (Numbers 26:5–51). The land is to be divided by size and by lot (Numbers 26:52–56), and the Levites are counted separately (Numbers 26:57–62). Not one man from the first count is left except Caleb and Joshua (Numbers 26:63–65).
Numbers 26.whereWeAre: The plague at Peor in chapter 25 has ended. Now God orders a second census, almost forty years after the first one in chapter 1. Only Caleb and Joshua are left from the old generation, and this new count will be used to divide the land.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Tells Moses and Eleazar to count the people again.

keyFigures.name: Moses and Eleazar
keyFigures.role: Count the new generation in the plains of Moab.

keyFigures.name: The tribes
keyFigures.role: Counted by families for dividing the land.

keyFigures.name: Caleb and Joshua
keyFigures.role: The only men left from the first count.

keyThemes.explanation: The people who left Egypt have died, and their children now stand ready.
Larger tribes receive more land.
The lot shows where each tribe's land will be.

Numbers 27.summary: The five daughters of Zelophehad ask for their father's land, since he had no sons, and God says, "The daughters of Zelophehad speak right" (Numbers 27:1–11). God tells Moses to look at the land from the mountain, for he will die without entering it (Numbers 27:12–14). Moses asks for a shepherd for the people, and Joshua is set apart before Eleazar and the congregation (Numbers 27:15–23).
Numbers 27.whereWeAre: The new generation was counted in chapter 26. Five daughters of Zelophehad ask for their father's share of the land, and God says yes. Then God tells Moses he will soon die, and Joshua is chosen to lead Israel into the land.

keyFigures.name: The daughters of Zelophehad
keyFigures.role: Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah, and Tirzah, who ask for their father's land.

keyFigures.name: Moses
keyFigures.role: Brings their case to the LORD and asks for a leader to follow him.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Grants their request and tells Moses he will soon die.

keyFigures.name: Joshua
keyFigures.role: Chosen to lead Israel after Moses.

keyFigures.name: Eleazar
keyFigures.role: The priest, before whom Joshua is set apart.

keyThemes.explanation: Five sisters ask for their father's land, and God says they are right.
Moses asks God for a leader, "that the congregation of the LORD be not as sheep which have no shepherd."
Joshua is given authority in front of the whole people.

Numbers 28.summary: God lists the offerings Israel must bring: a lamb every morning and evening (Numbers 28:1–8), extra offerings each Sabbath (Numbers 28:9–10), and offerings at the start of each month (Numbers 28:11–15). He gives the offerings for the Passover and the feast of unleavened bread (Numbers 28:16–25) and for the day of firstfruits (Numbers 28:26–31).
Numbers 28.whereWeAre: Joshua was named Moses' successor in chapter 27. Before Israel enters the land, God reminds the new generation of the offerings they must bring every day, week, month, and feast. The list of feasts continues in chapter 29.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Lists the daily, weekly, monthly, and spring offerings.

keyFigures.name: Moses
keyFigures.role: Commands the people to bring them.

keyThemes.explanation: A lamb is offered every morning and every evening.
Sabbaths and new moons have extra offerings.
The Passover and the firstfruits have their own offerings.

Numbers 29.summary: The seventh month begins with a day of blowing trumpets (Numbers 29:1–6), and its tenth day is a day to afflict their souls (Numbers 29:7–11). For the seven days of the feast that follows, the number of bulls drops by one each day, and an eighth day of assembly closes it (Numbers 29:12–38). These are in addition to vows and freewill offerings (Numbers 29:39–40).
Numbers 29.whereWeAre: Chapter 28 listed the daily, weekly, monthly, and spring offerings. This chapter covers the fall feasts of the seventh month: the blowing of trumpets, the Day of Atonement, and the feast of tabernacles. Chapter 30 turns to keeping vows.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Lists the offerings for the feasts of the seventh month.

keyFigures.name: Moses
keyFigures.role: Tells Israel all that the LORD commanded.

keyThemes.explanation: The seventh month has holy days with no ordinary work.
On the tenth day the people humble themselves before God.
The feast in the seventh month has offerings on every one of its days.

Numbers 30.summary: A man who makes a vow to the LORD must keep it (Numbers 30:1–2). A young woman's vow may be cancelled by her father on the day he hears it (Numbers 30:3–5), and a wife's by her husband (Numbers 30:6–8). A widow or divorced woman must keep her vow (Numbers 30:9), and a husband who stays silent lets his wife's vow stand (Numbers 30:10–16).
Numbers 30.whereWeAre: Chapters 28–29 covered the offerings Israel owes God. This chapter covers promises people make to God on their own. In chapter 31 Israel goes to war against Midian, the last task Moses must finish before he dies.

keyFigures.name: Moses
keyFigures.role: Tells the heads of the tribes the law of vows.

keyFigures.name: The heads of the tribes
keyFigures.role: Receive the law for their people.

keyThemes.explanation: A man who vows to the LORD must do "all that proceedeth out of his mouth."
A father or husband can cancel a vow on the day he hears it.
If he says nothing, the vow stands.

Numbers 31.summary: Twelve thousand men go to war against Midian, with Phinehas and the trumpets; they kill the five kings of Midian and Balaam (Numbers 31:1–12). Moses is angry that the women who led Israel into sin at Peor were spared, and he orders them killed (Numbers 31:13–18). Soldiers and spoil are made clean (Numbers 31:19–24), and the spoil is divided, with a share for the LORD (Numbers 31:25–47). The officers give an offering, because not one Israelite soldier was lost (Numbers 31:48–54).
Numbers 31.whereWeAre: God told Moses in chapter 27 that he would soon die. First, Israel must punish Midian for leading them into sin at Peor in chapter 25. After the battle, chapter 32 tells how two tribes ask to stay east of the Jordan.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Sends Israel to war against Midian.

keyFigures.name: Moses
keyFigures.role: Sends the army and is angry when the women are spared.

keyFigures.name: Phinehas
keyFigures.role: Goes with the army, carrying the holy things and trumpets.

keyFigures.name: The army
keyFigures.role: A thousand men from each tribe, who defeat Midian.

keyFigures.name: Balaam
keyFigures.role: Killed in the battle.

keyFigures.name: Eleazar
keyFigures.role: Teaches the soldiers how to make the spoil clean.

keyThemes.explanation: Israel punishes Midian for leading them into sin at Peor.
Soldiers and spoil must be made clean before coming back into the camp.
The spoil is counted and shared, with a portion for the LORD.

Numbers 32.summary: Reuben and Gad, who have great herds, ask to settle east of the Jordan (Numbers 32:1–5). Moses fears they are repeating the spies' sin (Numbers 32:6–15). They promise to fight with their brothers until the land is won (Numbers 32:16–19). Moses agrees but warns, "be sure your sin will find you out" (Numbers 32:20–32). Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh receive the land and build towns there (Numbers 32:33–42).
Numbers 32.whereWeAre: Israel has conquered the land east of the Jordan in chapter 21. Now the tribes of Reuben and Gad ask to settle there instead of crossing over. Moses fears a repeat of the spies' refusal in chapter 14, and after the matter is settled, chapter 33 looks back on the whole journey.

keyFigures.name: Reuben and Gad
keyFigures.role: Ask to settle east of the Jordan and promise to fight for their brothers.

keyFigures.name: Moses
keyFigures.role: Rebukes them, then agrees with a warning.

keyFigures.name: Eleazar and Joshua
keyFigures.role: Charged with seeing that the promise is kept.

keyFigures.name: The half tribe of Manasseh
keyFigures.role: Also given land east of the Jordan.

keyThemes.explanation: Moses asks, "Shall your brethren go to war, and shall ye sit here?"
Moses reminds them how the spies' fear kept a whole generation out of the land.

keyThemes.theme: Your sin will find you out
keyThemes.explanation: Breaking their promise would be a sin against the LORD.

Numbers 33.summary: Moses writes down every stop on Israel's journey, from Rameses to the plains of Moab, including Aaron's death on mount Hor (Numbers 33:1–49). God tells Israel to drive out the people of Canaan, destroy their idols, and divide the land by lot, or the people left will be "pricks in your eyes, and thorns in your sides" (Numbers 33:50–56).
Numbers 33.whereWeAre: Israel is camped on the plains of Moab, ready to cross the Jordan. Before they go, Moses writes down every stop on the journey from Egypt to here. Chapters 34–36 look ahead to dividing the land.

keyFigures.name: Moses
keyFigures.role: Writes down the stops on Israel's journey.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Tells Israel to drive out the Canaanites and divide the land.

keyThemes.explanation: The list traces every step of the forty years from Egypt.
Each family's land is to be chosen by lot.
Any Canaanites left in the land will bring trouble.

Numbers 34.summary: God describes the borders of the promised land, from the wilderness of Zin to the great sea and the Jordan (Numbers 34:1–12). The land is for nine and a half tribes, since the others have land east of the Jordan (Numbers 34:13–15). God names Eleazar, Joshua, and one leader from each tribe to divide it (Numbers 34:16–29).
Numbers 34.whereWeAre: Chapter 33 looked back over the whole journey from Egypt. Now God draws the borders of the promised land and names the leaders who will divide it. Chapter 35 sets aside towns for the Levites and cities of refuge.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Gives the borders of the land and names who will divide it.

keyFigures.name: Moses
keyFigures.role: Tells Israel the borders.

keyFigures.name: Eleazar and Joshua
keyFigures.role: Chosen to divide the land.

keyFigures.name: The tribal leaders
keyFigures.role: One from each tribe, chosen to help.

keyThemes.explanation: God draws the borders of the land he is giving.
Named leaders will divide the land fairly.
The tribes east of the Jordan already have their land, but they are still part of Israel.

Numbers 35.summary: The Levites are to receive forty-eight cities with land around them (Numbers 35:1–8). Six of them are cities of refuge for anyone who kills a person by accident (Numbers 35:9–15). The law separates murder from accidental killing, and the one who killed by accident stays in the city until the high priest dies (Numbers 35:16–29). A murderer needs more than one witness to be put to death, and no ransom may be taken for his life (Numbers 35:30–34).
Numbers 35.whereWeAre: Chapter 34 drew the borders of the land. This chapter gives the Levites forty-eight towns and sets apart six of them as cities of refuge for someone who kills by accident. Chapter 36 closes the book with one more question about land.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Gives the Levites' cities and the cities of refuge.

keyFigures.name: Moses
keyFigures.role: Passes the laws on to Israel.

keyThemes.explanation: Cities of refuge protect someone accused of killing until the case is judged.
The law separates a killing by accident from murder.
Bloodshed defiles the land, and no payment can excuse murder.

Numbers 36.summary: The leaders of Gilead's family worry that if Zelophehad's daughters marry into another tribe, their land will go with them (Numbers 36:1–4). Moses rules that they may marry whom they choose within their father's tribe (Numbers 36:5–9). The daughters marry their cousins, and their land stays in the tribe of Manasseh (Numbers 36:10–13).
Numbers 36.whereWeAre: This last chapter returns to the daughters of Zelophehad from chapter 27. Their tribe asks what happens to the land if they marry outside it, and God gives an answer that protects both. Numbers ends on the plains of Moab, and Deuteronomy records Moses' final speeches there.

keyFigures.name: The leaders of Gilead's family
keyFigures.role: Worry that their land will pass to another tribe.

keyFigures.name: Moses
keyFigures.role: Gives the LORD's ruling.

keyFigures.name: The daughters of Zelophehad
keyFigures.role: Marry their cousins so the land stays in Manasseh.

keyThemes.explanation: The daughters keep the land God gave them.
Marrying within the tribe keeps land from passing to another tribe.
"Even as the LORD commanded Moses, so did the daughters of Zelophehad."
